opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the questions I think about a lot, because the speedup from AI coding tools matters a lot for how fast AI R&D itself accelerates. Our scenario work leans heavily on the idea that once AI meaningfully speeds up the AI researchers, you get a feedback loop. So the empirical evidence on coding uplift is a key input.

The honest answer is that the evidence is messier than either side tends to admit. On one hand, you have lots of anecdotes and surveys where developers say these tools make them dramatically more productive, two times, five times, whatever. On the other hand, you have more careful studies. The one that got a lot of attention was METR's randomized controlled trial with experienced open-source developers working on their own repositories. They found that developers using AI tools were actually *slower*, something like 19 percent slower, even though the developers themselves believed they'd been sped up by roughly 20 percent. That gap between perceived and actual speedup is the most important finding, in my view. It means we should discount self-reports pretty heavily.

That said, I don't think that study settles things in the skeptics' favor either. It was a specific setting: very experienced people, large mature codebases they knew intimately, and tools from early 2025. That's probably close to the worst case for AI assistance. For someone working in an unfamiliar codebase, or writing lots of boilerplate, or doing quick experiments, the picture could look quite different. And the tools are improving fast. Agentic coding has gotten noticeably better since then, so a snapshot from a year or more ago can go out of date quickly.

So how do I update? A few things. First, I've become more skeptical of claims that we're already getting large speedups to AI research specifically. If the people closest to the work can't reliably perceive whether they're faster, then lab insiders saying "we're getting 2x from AI" should be treated with caution. That pushes me a bit toward longer timelines relative to the most aggressive versions of the story.

Second, though, the thing I care most about isn't the uplift from today's assistants. It's when AI systems can do long, autonomous chunks of research engineering end to end. METR's other line of work, measuring the length of tasks AI agents can complete, with that horizon doubling roughly every several months, is more directly relevant to that. Uplift studies measure humans plus tools. The transition I'm worried about is when the human stops being the bottleneck. You can have pretty modest uplift right up until the point where the agents become good enough to just do the job, and then things change quickly.

Third, I'd really like to see more of these studies run repeatedly, with the same methodology, as models improve. A single data point is hard to interpret. A time series of measured uplift, especially inside AI companies on actual research tasks, would be enormously valuable for forecasting. Ideally the companies would be measuring and publishing this, because it's exactly the kind of early warning signal for an intelligence explosion that policymakers and the public deserve to see.

So net, the evidence has made me somewhat less confident in the fastest timelines, but it hasn't changed my overall view that something like automating AI research this decade is a serious possibility we need to prepare for.

r001.rationale: The response describes the trial’s setting—experienced developers working in mature codebases they knew intimately—as “probably close to the worst case for AI assistance,” characterizing it as a particularly demanding test.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more important and more confusing pieces of evidence right now, and I want to be honest that it's cut against me in some ways.

So the backstory is that the whole AI 2027 scenario, and really most of the fast-timelines worldview, runs through this idea of an intelligence explosion that starts with AI automating AI research. And the first rung on that ladder is coding. If AI can't make AI researchers meaningfully more productive at writing code and running experiments, the whole feedback loop is a lot slower than we thought. So the question "are these tools actually speeding people up" is pretty load-bearing.

And then METR did this uplift study in 2025 where they took experienced open-source developers working on their own repositories, randomized whether they could use AI tools, and found that the developers were actually slower with AI, something like 19% slower, even though they believed they'd been sped up by 20-something percent. And I remember when that came out, my honest reaction was, okay, that's a real update. That's not the kind of result you get if we're a couple of years from automated AI researchers. So I pushed my timelines out somewhat, and I said so publicly.

But I'd put a few caveats on how much weight to put on it. One, the study was on a specific population: people who know their codebases extremely well, working on large, mature, high-standards repos. That's close to the worst case for current tools, because the thing the model is bad at is exactly context and taste about a codebase it hasn't seen. Two, those developers mostly had very little practice with the tools, and we know there's a learning curve. Three, the models have moved since then, and the agentic setups have moved even more. So I'd expect that if you reran that exact study today you'd get a different number, and I think the later METR work has pointed in that direction, though I don't want to overstate it.

The thing I try to do is not anchor on any single study, and instead ask: what does the whole picture say? And the whole picture is somewhat contradictory. You've got lab insiders saying things like "a large fraction of our code is now written by the models" and that they personally feel dramatically faster. You've got the METR time-horizon metric, where the length of task that models can do autonomously keeps doubling every several months, and that trend has if anything sped up. And then you've got careful RCTs showing modest or even negative uplift for some populations. Those can all be true at once. Self-reports are inflated, the metric measures something real but narrower than "doing the job," and the RCTs are measuring something real but on a slice of work that's hard for current tools.

So the way I'd frame it for timelines is: the coding speedup evidence is a lagging, noisy indicator of the thing I actually care about, which is whether the labs' internal R&D loop is accelerating. The leading indicator is the task horizon trend plus what the labs are actually doing with these systems internally. And on that I'd say the trend is still roughly on track, maybe a bit slower than my median in 2025, which is part of why my own numbers have drifted later, more like a few years out rather than 2027. But I wouldn't take "the RCT found no uplift" and conclude that the whole automation story is wrong. I'd take it as "the first rung is harder than it looked, and we should keep running the studies, because the moment it flips is the moment things get fast."

r001.rationale: The response calls the study setting “close to the worst case for current tools,” explaining that developers knew mature codebases extremely well and worked on high-standards repositories.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s relevant evidence, but there are several steps between “AI tools make coding faster” and “AI development is about to accelerate dramatically.” And I’d want to be careful about each of those steps.

First, what exactly are we measuring? Helping someone finish a well-specified programming task is different from helping them do their actual job, where they have to figure out what to build, understand an existing codebase, and check whether the result works. You can get impressive results on the first without getting equally impressive results on the second.

Then there’s the question of how much coding is the bottleneck in AI research. Even if you make writing code much faster, you might still be waiting for experiments to run, or struggling to decide which experiments are worth doing. So you can’t just take a coding speedup and apply that multiplier to the whole research process.

But I also wouldn’t take a disappointing result with today’s tools as strong evidence that we have lots of time. That tells us something about those tools, on those tasks, with those users. The thing we’re trying to forecast is when systems can carry out substantial research projects autonomously, including noticing mistakes and changing direction.

So I’d update on this evidence, but I’d put more weight on sustained improvements in realistic, end-to-end research work. Can a team actually get more useful experiments done? Can the AI take on longer projects with less supervision? Those seem much closer to the mechanism that could really shorten timelines.

r001.rationale: The candidate distinguishes well-specified coding tasks from realistic job work, but does not characterize the study finding that AI tools slowed coding as a particularly demanding test.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s relevant evidence, but you have to be careful about what exactly it’s evidence for. “How much do today’s AI tools speed up coding?” is different from “How far are we from AI systems that can automate AI research?”

For the first question, I’d want to look at the actual tasks and how people are using the tools. Are these experienced developers working in a codebase they know well? Are they doing relatively self-contained tasks? Does the measurement include the time spent checking and fixing the AI’s work? You could get quite different results in those different settings without any of the results being wrong.

For timelines, the thing I’m especially interested in is whether the systems can do longer and longer tasks autonomously. A tool that writes a function quickly but needs constant supervision is useful, but it’s a different proposition from a system you can give an experiment to, which then implements it, runs it, interprets the results, and figures out what to try next. That second thing could substantially accelerate AI development itself.

So, if we find that the tools aren’t producing much of a productivity improvement, that should update us somewhat towards longer timelines. We shouldn’t just explain away disappointing evidence. But I wouldn’t treat it as decisive, because it measures a particular deployment of current systems, and there could be a substantial gap between that and what the next generation can do. Equally, impressive speedups on selected coding tasks don’t establish that we’re about to automate research. I’d put more weight on a pattern of improving performance across increasingly long, realistic tasks than on any single headline productivity number.

r001.rationale: The response says disappointing productivity evidence should update timelines and notes that results vary by task, but it does not characterize a study finding of slower coding as a particularly demanding test.
